17-034.r: A Chief Minister who is a member of the State Legislative Council (Upper House) cannot vote for President; electoral college = elected MPs and elected MLAs of States, Delhi, Puducherry.

17-035.r: 'Population' for Presidential vote value = 1971 Census, until figures of the first census after 2026 are published (Article 81(3) proviso).

17-036.r: President eligibility (Article 58(1)): citizen of India, age 35 completed, qualified for election to Lok Sabha; no educational qualification.

17-037.r: President needs (Article 58(1)): citizenship (not necessarily by birth), age 35, and qualification for election to the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
17-037.t: Qualification is for the House of the People (Lok Sabha), not just 'Parliament'; citizenship need not be by birth.

17-038.r: Article 59(1): an MP or MLA elected President is deemed to vacate the seat on the date he enters upon office as President.

17-039.r: Article 57 → President is eligible for re-election any number of times.

17-040.r: Eligibility for re-election of the President → Article 57.

17-041.r: Disputes about Presidential election → decided by the Supreme Court (Article 71); its decision is final.

17-042.r: All three false: acts of a President whose election is voided by SC remain valid (Article 71(2)); election not postponed for Electoral College vacancies; no time limit for assent.

17-043.r: Article 56(1) → President's term is 5 years from the date he enters upon his office.

17-044.r: President addresses resignation to the Vice-President (Article 56(1)(a)), who at once informs the Lok Sabha Speaker (Article 56(2)).

17-046.r: President removed by Parliament through impeachment for violation of the Constitution (Article 56(1)(b), procedure Article 61); either House can start it.

17-048.r: All true: PR by single transferable vote, secret ballot (Article 55); nomination needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders; MLA vote value on 1971 census. Impeachment → Article 61.

17-053.r: Impeachment of President → Article 61: charge preferred by either House; the other House investigates; President may appear and be represented.

17-054.r: Article 61 → impeachment of President for 'violation of the Constitution' (not defined); quasi-judicial procedure in Parliament; either House can initiate.

17-058.r: Impeachment needs at least 14 days' written notice signed by at least one-fourth of total members of the House (Article 61(2)(a)).

17-059.r: State Legislative Assemblies elect the President but take no part in impeachment (only Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha do); Legislative Councils take part in neither.

17-060.r: Impeachment of President is a quasi-judicial process in Parliament only (Article 61); State Legislative Assemblies are in the electoral college (Article 54(b)) but not in impeachment.

17-062.r: Vacancy in President's office (death, resignation, removal) must be filled within six months (Article 62(2)).

17-065.r: Vice-President can act as President for at most 6 months, since a President's vacancy must be filled within 6 months.

17-066.r: Vacancy by death, resignation or removal → Vice-President acts as President until the new President enters office (Article 65(1)).

17-067.r: Both President and Vice-President offices vacant → Chief Justice of India acts as President; if absent, senior-most SC judge (President (Discharge of Functions) Act 1969).
hi: Chief Justice of India (भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश)

17-071.r: Article 361(2): no criminal proceedings against President or Governor during term; Article 361(4): civil proceedings allowed after two months' written notice. President is not above the Constitution.
17-071.c: No answer printed: A is only partly true (civil suits possible with notice) and R is false, so no option fits.

17-072.r: President dissolves Lok Sabha (Article 85(2)(b)) on the advice of the Union Cabinet / Council of Ministers headed by the PM (Article 74(1)).

17-074.r: Prorogation needs Council of Ministers' advice (statement 1 false); a House can be prorogued even in session; President dissolves Lok Sabha (Article 85(2)(b)), usually on Ministers' advice.

17-075.r: Joint sitting of both Houses → summoned by the President (Article 108); presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker (Article 118(4)).

17-078.r: Article 108: President notifies his 'intention' to summon a joint sitting when a Bill is rejected, amendments are disagreed, or six months pass without passing.

17-080.r: President is a constituent part of Parliament (Article 79), addresses a joint meeting every year, issues ordinances (Article 123); he does not take part in House discussions.

17-081.r: Both true, R explains A: Parliament = President + both Houses (Article 79); a Bill becomes law only with the President's assent (Article 111).

17-082.r: A Bill passed by Parliament becomes an Act only after the President's assent (Article 111).

17-083.r: Absolute veto (on Ministers' advice): Rajendra Prasad, PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954. Pocket veto (at discretion): Gyani Zail Singh, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill 1986.
17-083.t: The PEPSU Bill also saw a veto, but on Ministers' advice; the Post Office Bill pocket veto is the discretionary one the key wants.

17-084.r: Pocket veto (taking no action on a Bill) used only once: President Gyani Zail Singh, 1986, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.
17-084.h: Zail Singh kept the 'Post' in his pocket.

17-085.r: Article 111 → President declares assent to, or withholds assent from, a Bill passed by both Houses.

17-087.r: Discretionary: return a Bill with objections, withhold a Bill, send messages to Parliament (Article 86(2)). Appointing Ministers and judges = executive; summoning joint session = legislative power.

17-088.r: Per book, giving assent to Bills (Article 111) does not need Council of Ministers' advice; dissolving Lok Sabha, appointing ambassadors and other options do.

17-089.r: Promulgating ordinances (when Parliament is not in session) is the President's legislative power; Parliament must approve within six weeks of reassembly; President can withdraw it anytime.

17-090.r: President's discretion: return a Bill with objections, detain a Bill, seek information from the PM, ask Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice.

17-091.r: 2002 electoral reforms ordinance: President assented under Article 123 (ordinance power during Parliament's recess) after the Cabinet sent it back unchanged; ordinance has force of an Act.

17-092.r: Article 123 ordinances: same force as an Act of Parliament; must be approved within six weeks of reassembly; President can withdraw them any time ('can never repeal' is false).

17-094.r: President's ordinance must be laid before both Houses and ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles (Article 123(2)).

17-095.r: An ordinance can amend any Central Act (not the Constitution) and can be retrospective; it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights any more than an Act can.
17-095.c: Printed answer (a) I and II contradicts the explanation, which says II is incorrect and III correct, i.e. (c) I and III only.

17-096.r: President appoints Finance Commission Chairman (Article 280(1)) and UT Chief Ministers (Article 239AA(5)); Planning Commission Vice-Chairman was appointed by the PM (now NITI Aayog).

17-097.r: President appoints the Attorney General (Article 76), CAG (Article 148) and State Governors (Article 155).

17-098.r: Vice-President is elected (Article 66), not appointed by the President; PM, Governor and CEC are appointed by the President.

17-099.r: Article 160 → President may provide for discharge of a Governor's duties in any contingency.

17-100.r: A State's Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor (Article 164(1)), not by the President.

17-101.r: Article 143 → President may consult the Supreme Court on a question of law or fact; its advice is not binding on him.

17-103.r: Sending messages to Houses of Parliament (Article 86(2)) is a right of the President, not a 'power'; ordinances, consulting SC, pardon are powers.

17-104.r: President cannot remove a Supreme Court judge on his own: removal needs an address by each House with the required majority, then the President's order (Article 124(4)).

17-105.r: Pardoning power (Article 72: pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, suspend, remit, commute sentence) is a judicial power of the President.

17-106.r: Article 72 pardoning power: pardon, commutation, remission, respite, reprieve (also court-martial sentences); 'detention' and 'continuation' are not part of it.

17-107.r: Article 72 → President pardons for offences against Union law, court-martial sentences and all death sentences.

17-108.r: Pardoning power (Article 72) is open to limited judicial review; the President cannot use it without aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

17-109.r: President has titular (formal), de jure, constitutional and nominal authority, not real, popular or political authority.

17-110.r: President lays before Parliament: Finance Commission recommendations (Article 281), CAG report (151(1)), National Commission for SCs report (338(6)); not PAC report (a parliamentary committee).

17-111.r: President cannot return a Finance Bill for reconsideration (it needs his recommendation; not introduced in Rajya Sabha). Returning ordinary Bills, dissolving Lok Sabha, appointing PM are prerogatives.
